messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mere Tuilagi is a 66-year-old Fijian-American woman, divorced, who has owned and operated a small gift and import shop in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city for nearly two decades. She presented for intake with a PCL-5 score of 78, describing a prolonged period of deterioration following an incident of police violence that occurred approximately fourteen months prior to her first appointment.

The event took place on a weekday afternoon, in the late-golden light of early evening — the same hour at which Mere typically closed her shop and walked to her car in the adjacent lot. Officers responding to a reported disturbance in the area stopped her without warning, forced her to the ground, and restrained her with sufficient force to leave bruising across her wrists and face. She was alone. No one intervened. The physical pain was acute, but what she describes most haltingly — when she can describe it at all — is the sensation of being watched from the surrounding windows while she lay on the pavement, helpless and humiliated. She was released without charge.

In the weeks that followed, Mere found that the memory of the event refused to organise itself into anything coherent. There are portions she cannot retrieve at all, no matter how deliberately she reaches for them, and the fragments that do surface carry a quality of unreality — so extreme, she has told her therapist, that she sometimes wonders whether it truly happened to her. More distressingly, she cannot seem to put what occurred into words; when she attempts to recount it, language fails her entirely, and she is left with only a physical residue — a lurching dizziness, a sudden lightness in her head — that arrives without warning and without narrative context. This fragmented, wordless quality of the memory has itself become a source of alarm, because the gaps and the surreal texture of what she does recall now function as their own kind of cue: when a fragment surfaces, it pulls with it the full sensory weight of the original scene, and she is back on that pavement, certain she is being watched.

The hour of late afternoon has become almost unbearable. Each day, as the light in her shop shifts toward the angle it held that evening, Mere feels the dizziness rise and her attention fracture. To manage this, she has rearranged her closing time, asking her part-time assistant to lock up so that she herself leaves before the dangerous hour arrives. She avoids the parking lot entirely, parking two blocks away and varying her route. The anniversary of the incident — a date she cannot forget even as she tries to — she now spends away from the shop altogether, booking herself onto day trips or simply staying in bed with the curtains drawn. Over months, these strategies have narrowed her world considerably. A long-standing relationship with a neighbouring business owner has cooled; she no longer lingers after hours to share tea, and her absence has been noticed and misread as coldness. Occupationally, her reduced hours and her tendency to leave the floor to her assistant during the late-afternoon rush have begun to affect revenue.

What Mere had not anticipated was that the avoidance itself would feed what she was trying to escape. By never remaining in the shop at closing time, she has never been able to test whether she could tolerate it, and the hour has grown more menacing in her imagination. Her compulsive spending — sudden online purchases made late at night, a distraction that brings brief relief and later shame — has added a layer of self-reproach that compounds everything else. She has come to believe, with a quiet and devastating certainty, that she is inadequate: that a stronger woman would have recovered by now, that her continuing dizziness and her wordless terror and her inability to simply remember what happened and move past it are evidence that she is, as she put it in session, "losing her mind." The appraisal that she is a lousy coper and possibly going crazy has made her more reluctant to examine the memory directly, which in turn keeps it fragmented and unprocessed, which in turn keeps the triggers potent — and the loop draws tighter.

What finally brought Mere to seek help was a morning when she opened her shop, saw the afternoon light already beginning its slow shift, and found she could not make herself step inside. She stood on the pavement — the same posture, she realised, as that evening — and wept. She is most afraid that she is permanently changed. She is most hoping, she said quietly, that someone can help her find the words.
